title: Λύκος ⟨κεκορεσμένος⟩ καὶ πρόβατον
titleEn: The Sated Wolf and the Sheep
part: The Sated Wolf and the Sheep (Chambry 230 · Perry 159)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 230 (= Perry 159). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος τροφῆς κεκορεσμένος, ἐπειδὴ ἐθεάσατο πρόβατον ἐπὶ γῆς βεβλημένον, αἰσθόμενος ὅτι διὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ φόβον πέπτωκε, προσελθὼν παρεθάρσυνεν αὐτό, λέγων ὡς, ἐὰν αὐτῷ τρεῖς λόγους ἀληθεῖς εἴπῃ, ἀπολύσει αὐτό.
sentences.tr: Lykos trophēs kekoresmenos, epeidē etheasato probaton epi gēs beblēmenon, aisthomenos hoti dia ton heautou phobon peptōke, proselthōn paretharsynen auto, legōn hōs, ean autōi treis logous alētheis eipēi, apolysei auto.
sentences.l: A wolf sated with food, when he beheld a sheep flung down upon the ground, perceiving that it had fallen through fear of him, came up and kept encouraging it, saying that, if it should tell him three true statements, he would let it go.
sentences.i: A wolf who had eaten his fill saw a sheep lying flung on the ground, and, perceiving that it had collapsed out of fear of him, came up and reassured it, saying that if it told him three true things he would let it go.
sentences.n: κορέννυμι takes the genitive of what one has one's fill of, and κεκορεσμένος is the perfect: the state of being full, which is the fable's whole precondition. βεβλημένον is likewise perfect passive, 'thrown down and lying there.' διὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ φόβον is fear of him, not his own fear — the genitive of the person feared. The wolf's promise keeps the mood of his actual words, ἐάν with the subjunctive and a future indicative.

sentences.t: ⟨Τὸ⟩ δὲ ἀρξάμενον ἔλεγε πρῶτον μὲν μὴ βεβουλῆσθαι αὐτῷ περιτυχεῖν, δεύτερον δέ, εἰ ἄρα τοῦτο ἥμαρτε, τυφλῷ, τρίτον δὲ ὅτι « κακοὶ κακῶς ἀπόλοισθε πάντες οἱ λύκοι, ὅτι μηδὲν παθόντες ὑφ’ ἡμῶν κακῶς πολεμεῖτε ἡμᾶς. »
sentences.tr: ⟨To⟩ de arxamenon elege prōton men mē beboulēsthai autōi peritychein, deuteron de, ei ara touto hēmarte, typhlōi, triton de hoti « kakoi kakōs apoloisthe pantes hoi lykoi, hoti mēden pathontes hyph’ hēmōn kakōs polemeite hēmas. »
sentences.l: And ⟨it⟩, having made a beginning, said: first, that it had not wished to fall in with him; second, that if after all it had gone wrong in this, then with a blind one; and third: « wicked as you are, may you all perish wickedly, you wolves, because, having suffered nothing at our hands, you wickedly make war upon us. »
sentences.i: And the sheep began and said: first, that it had never wished to meet him; second, that if it had gone wrong in that after all, it would have wished him blind; and third: « Wretches, may you all come to a wretched end, all you wolves, since we have done you no harm and yet you make cruel war on us. »
sentences.n: ⟨Τὸ⟩ stands in angle brackets, Chambry's mark for a word he supplies himself — the neuter article for the sheep, πρόβατον being neuter, so the participles that follow are neuter too. The second answer is elliptical: τυφλῷ is a dative left hanging on the περιτυχεῖν of the first, 'to have met with him blind,' with the verb not repeated. The third ὅτι is not 'that' but the mark that direct speech follows, which is why Chambry opens his guillemets after it and the sheep turns to address the wolves as 'you.' κακοὶ κακῶς is the standard Greek jingle for a bad end — bad men, and badly. ἀπόλοισθε is an aorist optative of wish, the form a curse takes.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ λύκος ἀποδεξάμενος αὐτοῦ τὸ ἀψευδὲς ἀπέλυσεν αὐτό.
sentences.tr: Kai ho lykos apodexamenos autou to apseudes apelysen auto.
sentences.l: And the wolf, having approved its freedom from falsehood, let it go.
sentences.i: And the wolf, approving its truthfulness, let it go.
sentences.n: τὸ ἀψευδές is a neuter adjective used as an abstract noun, 'the not-lying' — Greek makes such nouns freely where English reaches for a suffix. ἀποδέχομαι is to accept a thing and think well of it.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλάκις ἀλήθεια καὶ παρὰ πολεμίοις ἰσχύει.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti pollakis alētheia kai para polemiois ischyei.
sentences.l: The story shows that often truth prevails even among enemies.
sentences.n: καί here is 'even,' not 'and' — the force of the moral hangs on it. παρά with the dative is 'in the presence of,' and so 'in the judgement of': truth carries weight even where the hearer is an enemy.
